You Tianxiao came into the Yuji native bank and went upstairs to report once more:

“There are men watching every part of the bank now. Each floor has hands posted, and the two doors, front and back, can be sealed on the word. We've borrowed an armored car from the garrison HQ's gendarmerie; parked in the middle of the road it's a fortress, and if they try to force their way through, let them run head-on into a wall.”
“Such a mustering of forces — didn't it alarm Director Mu?” Ye Qinian said lightly.
“Director Mu has gone to Nanjing; I'm afraid he won't be back till after the New Year.”

“Absurd. The government has ordered again and again that the offices are not to pay New Year calls on one another, not to take a holiday; yet some men forward the notices and issue the documents just the same, and never mend a single one of these feudal bad habits.”
“Director Mu has a great many relatives and friends in Nanjing; he's far busier there than he is here.”

“The Judge Advocate's office is a vital department, and certain men just hold down a post and do nothing. Mind you don't pick up these bad ways. Do good work, and when the chance comes I'll recommend you to those above.”

“Thank you, Teacher. But things as they are suit me well enough. Director Mu most likely finds the killing air of Longhua too heavy, bad for his official fortunes, and has no liking for the office's business; which makes it all the easier for me.”
Ye Qinian nodded, his face without expression.
“What are they doing in there just now?”

“We have five men in the main hall. Those two on the sofa in the deposit department are sitting back to back, so between them they can see the whole hall. The man and woman who went in are at the far end of the hall, with Assistant Manager Wu attending to them.”
“Tell your men not to get too close; let them get the suitcase without a hitch. We'll take them with the goods on them.”

“Yes, Teacher.” You Tianxiao said with a smile, “There's another odd thing. They've actually got someone sitting in the café at the mouth of Fucheng Li — a pickup point, I reckon. The man is Yi Junnian; I don't know what they mean by it.”

“Right there in Fucheng Li?” Ye Qinian laughed too. “We set our command post inside the Fucheng Li lane, and they set their pickup point at the mouth of the Fucheng Li lane — how droll. Your men going in and out at the lane mouth — will they be spotted by them?”
“I've told them: everyone is to stand at his assigned place and not go running about.”
“Chen Qianli still hasn't shown himself?”
“Our man posted at the Shenxin Hotel says that since he got back to his room in the middle of last night he hasn't come out at all. Shall we send someone in to take a look?”
“Someone keeping watch is enough. First get what's in the safe-deposit box, then arrest Lin Shi, and last of all haul in the whole net.”
Lin Shi took out the slip for safe-deposit box No. 279 and handed it to Assistant Manager Wu.
“Assistant Manager Wu, I'll open the box today. And here are three months' rent to give you.”

“Ah, Mr. Lin, a happy New Year to you —” Assistant Manager Wu's manner was a little unnatural. That morning at home he had had a telephone call from Mr. Song, telling him he must come to work today whatever else happened and see properly to the business of box No. 279. He did not know why this one box should so trouble Mr. Song; but Mr. Song had only told him to handle it as ordinary business, to do as the customer said, and that others would see to the rest: “We are a bank, neither the police nor the secret service; whoever comes to us is a customer. We must give no handle to gossip, let no one say that goods left in our care are not safe.”

With that word of Mr. Song's, Assistant Manager Wu felt sure of his ground. Mr. Song had never telephoned him in person before; indeed, even when Mr. Song came to the bank he never took the least notice of Assistant Manager Wu. But he knew quite well — in truth everyone in the bank, high and low, knew quite well — that Mr. Song's elder brother was a personage of the first importance. Otherwise, why should their small bank be able, year after year, to do a little of the Ministry of Finance's public-bond business?

Assistant Manager Wu got the papers in order and led Mr. Lin and his wife upstairs. The stairs were on the west side of the bank's main hall; on the second floor a gallery ran round all four sides, looking down on the hall, and Ling Wen swept it with her eyes.
Among the marble gallery pillars stood some sofas, and on a far one sat two men, quite alone, in a pair of Western suits that seemed not to fit them very well.
“By the bank's rules, only the customer who rents the box may enter the vault; Mrs. Lin can see her husband only this far.”

Ling Wen sat down on the sofa before the vault door and said to Assistant Manager Wu with a smile: “Mr. Lin's broken leg has only just healed and he moves with difficulty, so I'll leave him in your hands, Assistant Manager Wu.”

The vault entrance was on the south side of the second floor, its door ringed about with a grille, like an iron cage. Assistant Manager Wu opened the steel lock on the grille door with a key; within was another gleaming round door, welded from a single block of stainless steel. He turned the combination lock this way and that until there came a click, then spun the wheel at the center of the steel door several times, gave a gentle pull, and the vault door opened.

Assistant Manager Wu helped Lin Shi step through the round steel door; behind it was a vast stainless-steel cavern — the four walls, the floor and the ceiling all of steel plate, with light-tubes set into the seams that lit the square cavern bright as day. Deep in the cavern were rows of little rooms; Assistant Manager Wu ushered Lin Shi into one of them, in which stood a table and chairs. When Lin Shi had sat down, he said: “A moment, Mr. Lin, I'll just go down.”

The vault entrance was on the second floor, but the strongroom itself was underground. Assistant Manager Wu stepped into an elevator that held no more than two or three, and went down to the strongroom.

At a window seat in the Yiyuan Café, Yi Junnian ordered a cup of milk coffee, took out a newspaper and laid it on the table, and turned his head to watch the street. Beyond the window was a little courtyard set with a few sun umbrellas, folding tables and chairs beneath them, at which no one sat in the cold. The little courtyard had two gates, one giving onto Tianjin Road, the other onto the Fucheng Li lane.

On New Year's Day the café was all but empty of customers; the owner had not really meant to open for business at this hour, but as the banks and native banks roundabout were all working, he thought someone might come to sit a while. To this unlooked-for customer the owner sent over a pudding, on the house. On the pudding plate lay a little spoon, but the customer had not touched it.

“I went in and looked; Yi Junnian's still there. Our men saw him come across through the lane from Jiangxi Road; they seem to have a car parked over there. It's a Nanshi Police Bureau car.” You Tianxiao reported to Ye Qinian.

“Who told you to set your men watching so close? Nonsense — if you startle the snake in the grass —” Ye Qinian was not really angry; he sipped the good tea the native bank's proprietor had prepared, in a mood of no small self-content.

“So there are underground Party men in the Nanshi police after all.” Ever since the time an underground Party man had turned up in the Municipal Police at the market, You Tianxiao had begun to suspect there were Communists lurking in the Chinese-district police too. “Take him and follow the vine to the melon — we're sure to pull up a whole string. Your plan, Teacher, is truly brilliant; we just sit ourselves down here and the Communists pop up one by one.”
Ye Qinian was not so sanguine: “Communists are not a thing you can finish off by arresting. Arrest one, and they'll send you a dozen; arrest a dozen, and they'll send you a truckload.”

You Tianxiao thought to himself that the Teacher was about to launch into one of his long discourses; and, as in the days of the training class at Hangzhou, he brought his heels together and waited to receive the Teacher's instruction.

“In the struggle with the Communists, the most important thing is a cleansing of the mind. Only make people stop believing in that Communist creed and believe in our Three Principles of the People, and we win without a fight, and the Communist Party perishes without a fight. In your spare time you must read a little too; the books written by Professor Tao of Central University are very good. Read the books, grasp the reasoning in them, and when you interrogate Communists in the lockup you can reason with them and talk them into coming over to the government. In this way one tells ten, ten tell a hundred, a hundred tell a thousand; ideas are like a contagion — once infected, they become our people. Don't be forever beating men and killing men. Beating and killing can settle one man, a few men, but it can't settle the infection of the minds of tens of millions.”

Assistant Manager Wu came back up in the elevator, set the iron box he carried on the table, inserted a key, gave it a turn, and said to Lin Shi: “Mr. Lin, I've brought you the box; you've only to open it with your own key. When you've finished, press the electric bell on the table and I'll come back to let you out.”
With that he left the vault, closed the round steel door, and locked it again.
Not long after Assistant Manager Wu had left the vault, the lamp on the desk of Little Shi of the safe-deposit department lit up.

Earlier he had shown Mr. Ji into the vault. Mr. Ji was assuredly a great and wealthy personage: the guard-hairs standing out from his fur robe told at a glance it was a garment worth a fortune, no mere pelt of one or two beasts. Little Shi had seen Mr. Song's fur robe at Miss Tao's house, much like this one; he had a sharp eye, and a thing of value he had only to see once to remember.

That time had frightened him badly; in the end it was Miss Tao's quick wit that got him through, passing him off as her cousin. And out of that misfortune came a blessing: Mr. Song simply had him placed in the bank.

Little Shi had a clear head; he would never dare have any dealings of that sort with Miss Tao, though Miss Tao was forever having him up to her house to fetch a garment for her or buy a little something to eat. Miss Tao would be wearing a house jacket and knee-length shorts, a stretch of leg showing above her socks. Most bewitching of all were the two pink silk trouser-ties that fluttered below the short jacket, swaying to and fro at her every move. Once, as he sat on the sofa and she leaned over to speak to him, a silk tie actually brushed across his hand, and it was all he could do to master the impulse to give it a tug.

Little Shi opened the vault's steel door; Mr. Ji stood empty-handed behind it, waiting for him. He meant to see Mr. Ji to the bank's main door, for before going into the vault Mr. Ji had slipped him a silver dollar. Never in all his life had Little Shi taken so large a New Year's gift. But halfway there Mr. Ji told Little Shi that he was hard-pressed and must find a lavatory, and bade Little Shi not wait for him, as he would see himself out afterward.

Mr. Ji was none other than Chen Qianli. Though he had altered his appearance a little, he still feared being seen by the detective-squad plainclothesmen scattered through the building. He did not go into a lavatory, but slipped into the stairway the cleaning menials used, and went up and up to the rooftop terrace of the bank building, where he hid beside the water tank and observed the situation around the building. He noticed that the people going in and out of the Fucheng Li lane did not look like ordinary residents.

Ten-odd minutes later Lin Shi pressed the electric bell and called Assistant Manager Wu to open the door. Out of the vault, Ling Wen took the suitcase and helped Lin Shi step over the threshold. The two of them made their way along the gallery, down the stairs, and back into the bank's main hall under the eyes of the whole company.

Just as they were about to go out, a woman blew into the bank's main hall like a gust of wind, calling out the moment she was through the door: “Little Shi, come quick.” Little Shi, seeing her over there, hurried across. Ling Wen looked toward the voice, and it was, of all people, Miss Tao. Miss Tao recognized Ling Wen too, and finding there was no avoiding her, came over with a shamefaced air: “Ah, Mrs. Ling!” Her voice was overdone, and then all at once she dropped it low: “So you've got out too? I said to myself just now, the moment I stepped down from the rickshaw my heart went pit-a-pat, as if I were about to meet with some piece of good luck —”
As she spoke she raised a hand and pressed it to her heart.
“Miss Tao,” said Ling Wen, “thank you for carrying my letter for me.”
Miss Tao tried to cover her awkwardness: “Not at all, not at all, it was only on my way —”

On a sudden inspiration Ling Wen simply took Miss Tao by the arm and drew her over to the deposit counter, fished a little notebook from her bag, took a pen from the bank counter, and had Miss Tao write down her address, saying she must thank her properly. Miss Tao had known even in the lockup that Ling Wen too was the wife of a rich merchant; though the warders said she was a Communist, Miss Tao had always half doubted it, and now that she was out she must surely be in the clear — so she gladly wrote down a telephone number. The more Miss Tao talked the warmer she grew, and she saw Ling Wen all the way out of the bank. Cui Wentai sat in the car waiting for them.

Ling Wen set the suitcase she carried on the car's back seat and said a word to Cui Wentai: “You take the suitcase over.” Then she turned, shut the car door, and helped Lin Shi across the road, saying over her shoulder to Miss Tao as she went: “If you've time by and by, do come and have a slice of cake.”
“Cake, oh, I love cake, I love it . . .” Miss Tao ran on at cross-purposes, and before her words were even out she had already run back into the bank.

Cui Wentai started the car and drove on. He did not follow the route Chen Qianli had laid down, withdrawing by another road. He had, in fact, arranged it with Director Ye: the moment he had the suitcase he would drive the car straight into Fucheng Li and hand it to Captain You to inspect. No one had foreseen that they too would put their pickup point in Fucheng Li, that Ling Wen and Lin Shi, having crossed the road, would also be walking toward the mouth of the Fucheng Li lane. At this a taste he could not name rose in Cui Wentai's heart: this time, then, he was to go over to the enemy and turn traitor in the open street, in broad daylight?

He drove the car on a stretch, stopped a moment, then turned it around and drove back toward Tianjin Road. As the car neared the Fucheng Li lane, he suddenly swore aloud: “Go to hell, the lot of you — I'm going over to nobody, I'm going over to myself!”

He stamped hard on the gas, and the car went roaring past Fucheng Li. You Tianxiao, standing in the lane waiting to take delivery of the goods, never dreamed the car would go tearing by all at once, and was left there stranded and bewildered.
You Tianxiao rushed up the stairs and said to Ye Qinian: “Cui Wentai's run off with the suitcase.”
Ye Qinian nearly spat out a mouthful of tea; he thought a while, then swore all at once: “That swine — neither party, Nationalist nor Communist, has room for him.”
“Teacher, then do we make the arrests now or not?”

Ye Qinian thought a very long while: “Have your men keep up the watch; make no arrests for now. But you — go and get Cui Wentai back for me. The man, dead or alive, no matter; the suitcase is to be untouched, exactly as it was.”
